metaData.originalTitle: László Krasznahorkai Writes Because He Fails
metaData.title: László Krasznahorkai Writes Because He Fails
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: In an exclusive interview, Nobel laureate László Krasznahorkai discusses his evolving sentences, his obsession with failure, and the erosion of a sacred connection to beauty in modern technical civilization.
metaData.summary: This New Yorker interview with 2025 Nobel literature laureate László Krasznahorkai, conducted by Merve Emre, delves deep into his creative philosophy. Krasznahorkai explains how his notoriously long, spiraling sentences emerged from a desire to mimic „explosive confession“ in spoken language, an approach he developed after years of dissatisfaction with his own work. He reveals that he considers nearly all his books failures, a perfectionism that drives him to write. The conversation explores his central theme: the loss of a transcendent, sacred relationship to beauty in a disenchanted, pleasure-driven technical age. Krasznahorkai laments that while beauty endures (Michelangelo, the Acropolis), fewer people can truly experience it. He critiques the commodification of culture and the rise of traditionalist populism. The interview offers a rare, intimate portrait of a major literary figure's mind — his influences (Dostoevsky, Bach, Japanese art), his creative process (pacing rooms, composing sentences internally), and his melancholic yet sharp diagnosis of modern cultural crisis.

mainPoints.point: Krasznahorkai's long sentences mimic the 'explosive confession' of spoken language.
mainPoints.explanation: He argues that emotionally charged declarations cannot be broken into tidy sentences, which drove his shift toward fluid, confessional prose after middle age.

mainPoints.point: He considers all his books failures, which paradoxically compels him to keep writing.
mainPoints.explanation: This perfectionism is rooted in flaws he perceives in rhythm, melody, and form when forced to read his own texts aloud with film director Béla Tarr.

mainPoints.point: The sacred connection to beauty has been ruptured in modern technical civilization.
mainPoints.explanation: While beauty (art, nature) remains inviolable, contemporary humans can no longer experience it as transcendent due to commodification and a culture of pleasure.

mainPoints.point: Cultural populism distorts tradition into a political ideology, which he finds dangerous.
mainPoints.explanation: He criticizes the use of tradition to create enemies and laments that younger generations inherit a world where 'the entire occurrence of human civilization' as one epoch is over.

keyQuotes: I consider practically all of my books to have been failures, and if this sequence of failures had not occurred, I would have finished my career after my first book.

Everything that is beautiful—whether natural or created by human beings, whether created by God or by life itself—exists in an inviolable domain, which never changes. Only we change, only our relationship to this domain changes.
When a human being loses his sense of identity, there will be a need for so-called national identity and similarly idiotic ideas.

The first movement of despair, when a person is uncertain, when they feel frail, is to start looking for a form that will free them from this uncertainty, and then these political ideologies start coming very easily.

relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This New Yorker investigation reveals how Donald Trump's fantasy of annexing Greenland was pursued by a small group of ideologues and opportunists through covert influence operations, undermining NATO and the post-WWII world order.

relatedArticles.title: Jürgen Habermas Defended Reason in a Darkening Age
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article profiles Jürgen Habermas's life and philosophy, arguing that his defense of reason and the public sphere remains vital in an age of digital chaos and democratic backsliding.

relatedArticles.title: When Did White-Collar Work Start to Look So Bleak?
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article reviews three new books to trace the evolution of white-collar work from the aspirational yuppie era of the 1980s to the current climate of precarity and dread, linking the anxieties of today's graduates to historical shifts in corporate structure and economic promise.

relatedArticles.title: Audrey Wollen: “Is the Twenty-First Century a Cultural Void?”
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Audrey Wollen reviews W. David Marx's 'Blank Space' and argues that the perceived cultural void of the 21st century is not a lack of innovation but a different mode of creation, one defined by repetition, kitsch, and hauntology, which itself holds critical and emotional value.

relatedArticles.title: Instead of Taking Your Job， A.I. Might Transform It
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article argues that AI is not primarily a job-replacing automation technology, but rather a tool that empowers workers to create bespoke, intern-like software, transforming their roles instead of eliminating them.
